Spoken English Starter and Elocution Basics: ten short topics each,
linked one by one from the 'I am Learning Spoken English' and
'I am an Elocution Student' routes on the home page (the #anchors must
Everything is written by RCF English: every dialogue, tongue twister,

pages.title: Spoken English Starter
pages.metaTitle: Spoken English for Beginners: 10 Everyday Topics with Phrases and Conversations
pages.description: Start speaking English with ten everyday topics, from greetings to small talk. Each has the phrases you need and a short conversation to hear and practise.
pages.keywords: spoken English for beginners, everyday English phrases, basic English conversation, spoken English Sri Lanka, English greetings, English for shopping, telephone English

hero.text: Ten everyday topics, one at a time. Learn a few phrases, hear them in a short conversation, then take a part and say it yourself.

items.title: Read the phrases
text: Say each one aloud twice.

items.title: Play the conversation
text: Listen for the phrases you have just read.

items.title: Take a part
text: Press a name, and speak that person's lines.

items.title: Use it today
text: Try one phrase in real life before tomorrow.

blocks.heading: 1. Greetings and introducing yourself
text: The first few words of a conversation matter most. Keep them short, smile, and use the other person's name if you know it.

rows: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
Hello, I'm Ruwan. Nice to meet you.

items.title: A new neighbour
items.setting: Ruwan has just moved into a new house and meets his neighbour.

lines.speaker: Ruwan
lines.text: Good morning! I'm Ruwan. I've just moved in next door.

lines.speaker: Mrs Perera
lines.text: Oh, hello, Ruwan. I'm Mrs Perera. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Ruwan
lines.text: Nice to meet you too.

lines.speaker: Mrs Perera
lines.text: Welcome to the street. If you need anything, just ask.

lines.speaker: Ruwan
lines.text: Thank you, that's very kind of you.

blocks.heading: 2. Talking about your family
text: Family is one of the first things people ask about. Use *have*, *is* and *live* to describe who is in your family.

rows: I have one brother and two sisters.
I'm the eldest. / I'm the youngest.
My father is a farmer, and my mother is a nurse.
Do you have any brothers or sisters?

items.title: At a friend's house
items.setting: Two classmates are talking while they wait for lunch.

lines.speaker: Sachini
lines.text: Do you have any brothers or sisters, Amal?

lines.speaker: Amal
lines.text: Yes, I have one older brother. He works in Colombo. What about you?

lines.speaker: Sachini
lines.text: I have two younger sisters, so I'm the eldest.

lines.speaker: Amal
lines.text: That must be busy! Do you all live together?

lines.speaker: Sachini
lines.text: Yes, and my grandmother lives with us too.

blocks.heading: 3. Your daily routine
text: Use the present simple for things you do every day, with words such as *usually*, *always* and *on Sundays*.

rows: I usually get up at six o'clock.
I go to work by bus.
After dinner, I watch the news.
On Sundays, I relax at home.

items.title: A busy day
items.setting: Two colleagues are talking during a tea break.

lines.speaker: Dinesh
lines.text: You always look so fresh in the morning. What time do you get up?

lines.speaker: Harsha
lines.text: At half past five. I go for a short walk before work.

lines.speaker: Dinesh
lines.text: Half past five! I usually get up at seven.

lines.speaker: Harsha
lines.text: But you go to bed late, don't you?

lines.speaker: Dinesh
lines.text: Yes. I usually watch television until midnight.

blocks.heading: 4. Shopping
text: In a shop, a few polite questions will get you everything you need.

rows: Do you have this in a bigger size?
When you don't need help yet

items.title: Buying a shirt
items.setting: Nuwan is in a clothes shop.

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.text: Good afternoon. Can I help you?

lines.speaker: Nuwan
lines.text: Yes, please. How much is this blue shirt?

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.text: It's two thousand five hundred rupees.

lines.speaker: Nuwan
lines.text: Do you have it in a bigger size?

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.text: Yes, here's a large. The changing room is over there.

lines.speaker: Nuwan
lines.text: Thank you. Can I pay by card?

lines.speaker: Shop assistant
lines.text: Of course.

blocks.heading: 5. Ordering food
text: *I'd like...* is the most useful phrase in any restaurant. It is polite, and it works for everything on the menu.

rows: Could we see the menu, please?
I'd like rice and curry, please.
Could I have a glass of water, please?
Could we have the bill, please?

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Are you ready to order?

lines.speaker: Thilini
lines.text: Yes. Is the chicken curry very spicy?

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: A little. The vegetable curry is milder.

lines.speaker: Thilini
lines.text: Then I'd like rice with vegetable curry, please.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: And to drink?

lines.speaker: Thilini
lines.text: Could I have a lime juice, please?

blocks.heading: 6. Asking for directions
text: Start with *Excuse me*, and do not be afraid to ask the person to repeat. Repeating the directions back is the best way to be sure.

rows: Excuse me, where is the bus stand?
Go straight on, then turn left.
It's next to the bank. / It's opposite the school.
Sorry, could you say that again?

items.title: Finding the post office
items.setting: Kumari is visiting a new town.

lines.speaker: Kumari
lines.text: Excuse me, is there a post office near here?

lines.speaker: Passer-by
lines.text: Yes. Go straight on and take the second road on the right. It's opposite the school.

lines.speaker: Kumari
lines.text: Sorry, could you say that again?

lines.speaker: Passer-by
lines.text: Straight on, second on the right. It's opposite the school.

lines.speaker: Kumari
lines.text: Second on the right. Thank you very much!

blocks.heading: 7. On the telephone
text: On the phone, nobody can see you, so say who you are and speak a little more slowly than usual.

rows: May I speak to Ms Fernando, please?
Could you hold on a moment, please?
She isn't here. Can I take a message?
When the person is not there
Could you speak a little louder, please?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Good morning, Lanka Traders. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: Nimal
lines.text: Hello, this is Nimal Silva speaking. May I speak to Ms Fernando, please?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: I'm sorry, she's in a meeting. Can I take a message?

lines.speaker: Nimal
lines.text: Yes, please. Could you ask her to call me back this afternoon?

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.text: Of course. Could I have your number, please?

lines.speaker: Nimal
lines.text: It's zero seven seven, one two three, four five six seven.

blocks.heading: 8. Asking politely
text: *Could you...?* and *Would you mind...?* turn an order into a request. In English, politeness is often in the question, not just in *please*.

rows: Would you mind closing the window?
Of course. / Sure, here you are.
Sorry, I'm using it right now.

items.title: In the classroom
items.setting: Two students are sitting together in a lesson.

lines.speaker: Pradeep
lines.text: Anusha, can I borrow your ruler, please?

lines.speaker: Anusha
lines.text: Sure, here you are.

lines.speaker: Pradeep
lines.text: Thanks. And would you mind explaining question three? I don't understand it.

lines.speaker: Anusha
lines.text: Not at all. Look, you need to find the area first.

lines.speaker: Pradeep
lines.text: Oh, I see now. Thank you!

blocks.heading: 9. Thanking and apologising
text: *Thank you* and *sorry* are small words that make a big difference. Learn the replies too, so the conversation can move on.

items.title: A late arrival
items.setting: Kasun arrives late to meet a friend.

lines.speaker: Kasun
lines.text: I'm so sorry I'm late. The bus was very slow.

lines.speaker: Dilani
lines.text: That's all right. I only got here ten minutes ago.

lines.speaker: Kasun
lines.text: Thanks for waiting. Let me buy you a cup of tea.

lines.speaker: Dilani
lines.text: Oh, thank you! That's kind of you.

lines.speaker: Kasun
lines.text: It's the least I can do.

blocks.heading: 10. Small talk: the weather and weekend plans
text: Small talk is friendly conversation about easy topics. It fills a silence, and it often starts a real conversation.

rows: I'm going to visit my cousins.
Have a nice weekend! / You too.

lines.speaker: Roshan
lines.text: It's really hot today, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Yes, I think it's going to rain later.

lines.speaker: Roshan
lines.text: Any plans for the weekend?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: I'm going to visit my cousins in Kandy. What about you?

lines.speaker: Roshan
lines.text: Nothing special. I'm just going to relax at home.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Sounds good. Have a nice weekend!

lines.speaker: Roshan
lines.text: You too!

text: Order at a café, buy a ticket or ask for directions, and the website answers what you say.

pages.title: Elocution Basics
pages.metaTitle: Elocution Basics: Posture, Breathing, Tongue Twisters, Reading Aloud and Speaking with Confidence
pages.description: Ten elocution topics with exercises: posture, breathing, voice warm-ups, tongue twisters, word stress, intonation, pace and pausing, and reading a poem aloud.
pages.keywords: elocution for beginners, elocution exercises, tongue twisters for clear speech, reading aloud practice, voice projection, public speaking for students, elocution Sri Lanka

hero.text: Elocution is the art of speaking clearly, expressively and with confidence. Ten short topics, each with an exercise you can do in five minutes.

blocks.title: About this page
text: These are general exercises in clear, confident speaking, written by RCF English. They are not the syllabus of any elocution examination. If you are preparing for an examination, follow the syllabus your teacher gives you.

blocks.heading: 1. Posture: stand well to speak well
text: Your voice comes from your whole body. If you slump, your chest cannot fill with air and your voice sounds weak.

parts.heading: Exercise
numbered: Stand with your feet a little apart, your weight even on both feet.
Let your arms hang loosely. Roll your shoulders back and down twice.
Imagine a string pulling the top of your head gently up towards the ceiling.
Keep your chin level: not up in the air, not down on your chest.
Say *Good morning, everyone* in this position. Then slump and say it again. Hear the difference.

blocks.heading: 2. Breathing for speech
text: Good speakers breathe low, from the stomach, not high in the shoulders. Low breathing gives you more air and a steadier voice.

parts.heading: Exercise
numbered: Put one hand on your stomach, just below your ribs.
Breathe in slowly through your nose. Your hand should move out; your shoulders should not rise.
Breathe out slowly on a long *ssss* sound, as if letting air out of a tyre.
Now breathe in, and count aloud from one to ten on a single breath.
Each day, try to count one number further, without rushing or straining.

blocks.heading: 3. Warming up your voice
text: Singers warm up before they sing, and speakers should too. Two minutes is enough.

parts.heading: Exercise
numbered: Yawn widely, then sigh out gently on *haaa*. This relaxes your throat.
Hum *mmmm* with your lips closed. Feel the buzz on your lips and nose.
Blow air through loose lips so they flutter, like a motorbike: *brrrr*.
Move your jaw gently from side to side, then open and close it slowly.
Say *ma, me, mi, mo, mu*, opening your mouth clearly for each sound.

blocks.heading: 4. Tongue twisters for clear speech
text: Tongue twisters train your lips, tongue and teeth to move quickly and precisely. Say each one **slowly and clearly three times first**, then a little faster. Clarity always matters more than speed.

blocks.heading: Ten tongue twisters to practise
blocks.caption: Written by RCF English.
rows: Big black buses bring back busy boys.
Priya put plenty of pink paper plates in a plastic box.
Tall Tom tied ten tidy knots today.
Seven silver spoons sit safely on the shelf.
Shanthi's shiny shoes slipped on the shop's smooth steps.
Three thin thinkers thought through thirty things.
Vimal's van waited while Wimal washed the windows.
Five friendly farmers fed fresh fruit to fifty foxes.
Red roses rarely grow along long lonely lanes.
Good cooks cook great cakes quickly.

blocks.title: Check yourself
text: Record yourself on your phone and listen back. Can you hear every sound? The [Speaking Practice read-aloud exercises](speaking-practice/?mode=read) also show which words were recognised.

blocks.heading: 5. Short and long vowel sounds
text: Many words change their meaning when a vowel is short or long. Say each pair aloud, making the difference clear. Keep the long sound long, without rushing it.

rows: The sheep are on the ship.
Don't be a fool: the bus is full.
The baby was caught climbing out of the cot.
Fill the glass and feel how cold it is.
Pull the child out of the pool.
He dropped his cap into the carp pond.

blocks.heading: 6. Word stress
text: In English, one part of a longer word is said more strongly: a little louder, longer and higher. Stress in the wrong place can make a word hard to understand. The stressed part is in capital letters below.

rows: record (a noun: a record of marks)
record (a verb: to record a song)

blocks.heading: 7. Stress and intonation in sentences
text: In a sentence, we stress the words that carry the meaning, and our voice rises and falls. This is what makes speech sound alive rather than flat.

parts.heading: The tune of a sentence
bullets: **Statements fall at the end:** I live in Galle. ↘
**Yes/no questions usually rise:** Do you live in Galle? ↗
**Wh- questions usually fall:** Where do you live? ↘
**Lists rise, rise, then fall:** I bought rice ↗, dhal ↗ and onions. ↘

parts.heading: Exercise: move the stress, change the meaning
text: Say this sentence five times, stressing a different word each time. Notice how the meaning changes.
numbered: **SHE** gave me the red book. (not someone else)
She **GAVE** me the red book. (it was a gift, not a loan)
She gave **ME** the red book. (not you)
She gave me the **RED** book. (not the blue one)
She gave me the red **BOOK**. (not the red pen)

blocks.heading: 8. Pace and pausing
text: Nervous speakers rush. A pause gives your listeners time to understand, and gives you time to breathe. In the passage below, **/** means a short pause and **//** means a longer pause. Read it aloud slowly, then read it again without the marks, keeping the pauses.

parts.heading: Practice passage
text: *Every morning / before the town wakes up / an old man walks along the beach. // He carries a small bag / and a long stick. // He is not looking for shells. / He is picking up plastic. // When people ask him why, / he smiles / and says, / "Somebody has to start." //*

parts.heading: Tips
bullets: Pause at full stops and commas, and before an important word.
Slow down for names, numbers and the most important sentence.
A pause that feels long to you usually sounds natural to your audience.

blocks.heading: 9. Reading aloud with expression
text: Reading aloud well means understanding the words first, then letting your voice show their meaning. Read the poem silently, decide how it should sound, and then read it aloud.

parts.heading: Before you read
numbered: Read the whole piece silently, and make sure you understand every word.
Decide the mood: happy, sad, calm, excited or funny?
Pause at punctuation, not at the end of every line.
Choose one or two words in each line to stress.
Look up from the page now and then, to connect with your listeners.

parts.heading: Practise with this poem: The Monsoon Comes
text: *All morning the sky was heavy and grey,*
*the crows were quiet, the dogs would not play.*
*Then one cool wind ran over the hill,*
*the palm trees shivered, and then stood still.*
*A drop on a leaf. A drop on my hand.*
*A drumming of rain on the thirsty land.*
*And down by the river, loud and free,*
*the frogs began singing their thanks with me.*
Poem written by RCF English.

parts.heading: How to read it
bullets: **Lines 1 and 2:** slow and low, to show the heavy, waiting sky.
**Lines 3 and 4:** a little faster, as the wind arrives; pause after *shivered*.
**Line 5:** short pauses after each sentence, like single raindrops.
**Line 6:** pick up speed and volume for the drumming rain.
**Lines 7 and 8:** bright and joyful, ending with a warm smile in your voice.

blocks.heading: 10. Speaking to an audience
text: Everyone feels nervous before speaking in front of people. Good speakers are not free of nerves; they have simply learned what to do with them.

parts.heading: Before you speak
bullets: Practise aloud at least three times, once in front of a friend or a mirror.
Take two slow, low breaths before you begin.
Stand still with your weight on both feet, and smile.

parts.heading: While you speak
bullets: Look at different people in the audience, a few seconds each.
Use your hands naturally, to show size, number or feeling.
Speak a little more slowly and loudly than in conversation.
If you forget a word, pause, breathe, and carry on. The audience rarely notices.

parts.heading: A one-minute speech plan
numbered: **Greeting:** *Good morning, teachers and friends.*
**Topic:** *Today I would like to talk about...*
**Point one, with an example.**
**Point two, with an example.**
**Ending:** *So, let us all... Thank you for listening.*
